item.description: How to buy a house in the Canton of Basel-Country: guide to the three tax levels, mortgage and hidden costs

## In a nutshell - Three tax levels: federal, cantonal, municipal - Mortgage loan requires at least 20% equity - Transfer tax is a cantonal tax - Notary fees and ancillary costs affect the total
## Key facts - What: Purchase of a house in the Canton of Basel-Country - Where: Canton Basel Country, northwestern Switzerland - Who: Resident and non-resident buyers - Tax levels: Three (federal, cantonal, municipal) - Transfer tax: Cantonal tax at the time of purchase
The system of buying a house in the Canton of Basel-Country follows Swiss national rules, but with particular cantonal and municipal taxation. Unlike many European systems, Switzerland applies a system of direct taxation at three levels: the federal level (Swiss Confederation), the cantonal level (Canton Basel-Country) and the municipal level. Each level has competence over different taxes, and in the Canton each municipality can apply a multiplier on a cantonal basis. The [dichiarazione annuale delle imposte](nav:tax-return) follows the Swiss national model.
Buying a house in the Canton of Basel-Country means dealing not only with the purchase price, but also with related costs such as the transfer tax (a cantonal tax), notary fees (charged by the profession) and, once owners, with the annual tax burden linked to real estate ownership.

Buying a home in the Basel-Country Canton almost always requires a mortgage. At the Swiss national level, the mortgage sustainability criteria follow common principles:
- LTV (Loan-to-Value) ratio: Swiss banks usually require a maximum mortgage-to-value ratio of around 80%, which means that the buyer must have at least 20% of the purchase price. - Repayment capacity: Banks assess the sustainability of the mortgage based on the borrower's income and other financial obligations. The common criterion is that the mortgage installment does not exceed 33% of the monthly net income. - Term of the loan: Generally between 15 and 30 years, with the possibility of early repayment.
In the canton of Basel-Country, as in the other cantons, interest rates on mortgages are determined by the market (influenced by the Swiss National Bank — SNB/SNB) and are not fixed by cantonal legislation. However, sustainability assessment criteria may vary slightly from bank to bank, even if they follow common guidelines of the Swiss Bankers' Association. ## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Procedure step-by-step for purchasing in the Canton Basel-Landschaft
The purchasing procedure of a property in the Canton Basel-Landschaft follows standardized national Swiss steps, with cantonal specifics:
1. Search and offer: Identify the property and submit a binding offer to the seller. In Switzerland, there is no mandatory legal exclusivity period during the negotiation.
2. Preliminary (Vorvertrag): Once the offer is accepted, the parties sign a preliminary agreement that specifies the price, delivery date, and suspensive conditions, such as obtaining a mortgage.
3. Mortgage: Request a mortgage from the bank. The process includes property valuation, mortgage sustainability check, and signing the mortgage promise.
4. Notary: Once all details are finalized, the parties visit the notary to sign the definitive deed (Kaufvertrag). The notary registers the deed in the cantonal land register and calculates the transfer tax.
5. Property transfer: The notary registers the property transfer in the cantonal land register. At this point, the mortgage is disbursed, and the seller receives the payment.
### Transfer tax: timing and calculation
The transfer tax in the Canton Basel-Landschaft is calculated by the notary at the time of signing the definitive deed. It is a cantonal tax, meaning the rate and calculation methods are set by cantonal legislation, not federal law. The amount varies based on the purchase price and any applicable exemptions or benefits under cantonal laws, such as exemptions for the purchase of the primary residence in some cantons or reductions for spouses.
Typically, the transfer tax is paid at the time of signing the definitive deed by the notary or can be paid according to the modalities established by the canton.
### Notarial fees
Notarial fees in the Canton Basel-Landschaft are set by the notarial profession's tariff, not by federal law. They include: drafting the purchase deed, registration in the land register, legal advice, and administrative costs.
These fees are normally borne by the buyer (unless otherwise agreed with the seller) and represent, on average, 1-2% of the purchase price, depending on the complexity of the transaction.
### Additional costs: Registration fee and stamp duty
In addition to transfer tax and notarial fees, consider:
- Registration fee for the land register: A cantonal tax for registering the property in the land register.
- Valuation costs: If required by the bank for the mortgage.
- Property insurance: Mandatory if the mortgage exceeds a certain threshold. It covers property damage (fire, theft, etc.).
All these costs should be factored into the purchase planning to avoid liquidity shortfalls in the final phase.
### Final checklist before purchase
Before proceeding with the purchase, it is advisable to verify:
- Mortgage sustainability (LTV ratio, repayment capacity)
- Availability of own funds (at least 20% of the purchase price)
- Cantonal transfer tax estimate
- Notarial fee estimate
- Annual fiscal burdens as a property owner
- Property insurance coverage
Seeking the advice of a real estate consultant or notary for reviewing these aspects is highly recommended, especially if it is the first time purchasing a property in Switzerland.

## In a nutshell - The L permit allows temporary work in Switzerland for up to 1 year, renewable - Remains linked to the employer: change of employment requires new application - Pass to non-automatic B permit; requires proven occupational stability
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term leave for foreign workers in Switzerland - Maximum validity: 1 year (renewable according to SEM-cantonal assessments) - Competence: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) + cantonal authority - Main constraint: Linked to the employer specified in the request - Transition: Towards permit B (residence) if proven occupational stability
## # What is Short Term L Permit
The L permit is a temporary work permit issued by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) and the competent cantonal authority for foreigners wishing to carry out a professional activity in Switzerland. This is the shortest solution among Swiss migratory statuses: the maximum validity is 1 year, with the possibility of extension according to the procedures defined by federal laws on migration.
Unlike the B residence permit (renewable) and the C residence permit (normally issued after 10 years of permanent residence in the country), the L permit is designed as a temporary bridge for foreign workers who do not intend to settle permanently in Switzerland, or who do not yet have the requirements for a permanent ### Extension and renewal of permit L
The extension of the L permit beyond the first year is not automatic. The SEM and cantonal authorities assess each renewal request on a case-by-case basis, considering factors such as the continuity of employment, the economic situation of the employer, the absence of grounds for refusal (deficiencies in the payments of AVS/AI contributions, debts to the tax administration, etc.).
The maximum number of consecutive years during which it is possible to maintain an L permit varies according to specific circumstances, but the federal law establishes principles of temporaryity: the L permit is conceived as a bridging solution, not as a permanent status. If the worker wishes to settle in Switzerland beyond the initial term and renewals of the L permit, he/she will have to move towards the B (residence) permit, which is renewable and offers more favourable employment conditions.
### Transition from permit L to permit B
The transition from permit L to permit B takes place when the worker demonstrates lasting occupational and personal stability in the canton. There is no automatic right to this transition: the application for permit B must be evaluated by the SEM and cantonal authorities according to the specific federal and cantonal criteria.

item.title: Permit L in Basel Countryside: validity and extension
item.description: The L permit allows work for up to 12 months in Basel-Country. Discover maximum duration, renewal rules, transition to permit B and employer constraints.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit L: maximum validity 12 months, renewable - Closely related to the specified employer - Managed by SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) and canton - Transition to permit B after 12 months of uninterrupted work
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term L leave for foreign employment - When: Valid for 12 months, renewable annually - Where: Canton Basel-Country, northern Switzerland - Who: SEM and Cantonal Migration Office - Requirements: Employment contract with Swiss employer, documentation
The short-term L permit allows foreign nationals to work in Switzerland for up to 12 months. In the Basel-Country Canton the permit is managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) in coordination with the local authorities. It is not an automatic permit: it requires a formal request from the employer to the competent cantonal authorities.
A key feature of the L permit is the constraint on the employer and the canton of employment specified in the initial application. The worker cannot freely change employer without a new procedure, nor move to another canton without a change request. This constraint reflects the temporary and sectoral nature of the permit, designed to meet specific work needs.
### Structure and maximum duration
Validity is limited to 12 months from the date of issue. The permit is renewable if the employment relationship ### Maximum duration and renewal mechanism
The L permit is structured for temporary and short work needs. The 12 months of validity are non-negotiable: any initial request cannot exceed this period. If the employment relationship continues, the permit can be renewed several times, theoretically without limit, until the employer requests its renewal.
Renewal is not automatic. The employer must submit a new application at least 30 days before the expiry of the current permit. If this request is not submitted, the permit expires and the worker loses the right to stay and work in Switzerland. It is the responsibility of the employer (with the support of the cantonal authorities) to manage administrative time to avoid interruptions.
### Conditions for extension
The extension of the L permit depends on administrative and economic factors. The Canton of Basel-Country assesses the continuity of the employment relationship and consistency with the needs of the local labour market. If the employer proves to continue to need the foreign worker and if there are no violations of the law, the renewal is usually approved.
However, renewal can be denied if the employer ceases the activity or changes legal form, there are breaches in the payment of contributions (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% for the employee, 10.6% total with the employer), the worker has violated the conditions of permanence (for example he worked for another employer without
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to request the L permit: step-by-step procedure The L permit request starts with the employer, not the employee. The Swiss employer must initiate the process with the competent authorities of the Canton Basel-Country, usually the cantonal migration office.
Phase 1: Preparation of the documentation. The employer prepares the file containing a copy of the employment contract (with workplace, job description, duration, salary), the employee's foreign identity documents (passport, residence certificates if required), good conduct certificates in some cases, and company documentation (commercial registration, statutes).
Phase 2: Submission of the request to the canton. The employer submits the file to the competent cantonal authority in Basel-Country responsible for work permits (usually the Migration Office or Population Office). SEM intervenes in a consultative capacity for non-EU/EFTA citizens.
**Phase 3: Evaluation and issuance.** The cantonal authority examines the request, verifies the local labor market situation, and approves or rejects it within 2-6 weeks. If approved, the L permit is issued with a validity period of 12 months from the date of issuance.
### Critical deadlines: what to remember The L permit has clearly indicated start and end dates on the document. Renewal must be requested at least 30 days before the expiration date. If the employer forgets this deadline, the permit expires, and the employee can no longer work legally in Switzerland.
For renewal, the procedure is similar to the initial request, but faster (usually 2-4 weeks) since the canton already has the data on file. The employer submits a request for extension, attaching confirmation of the continued employment relationship (employer's letter), an updated copy of the contract if modified, and a certificate of contributions paid (AVS/AI/IPG and invalidity insurance).
### Social contributions and administrative obligations The L permit is issued free of charge by the canton. However, the employer is required to pay social contributions: AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% for the employee (10.6% total with the employer), AD/AC at 1.1% up to the annual maximum. Additionally, they must insure the employee with a mandatory health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of the start of work and pay SUVA contributions (if relevant to the sector).

item.title: Offline credit card payments since 2027 in Switzerland
item.description: From 2027, Swiss stores will be able to process credit and debit card payments even without the internet. DEFR, the SNB and the Federal Council announce the solution for financial resilience.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - From 2027 offline payments with credit cards in Swiss stores - DEFR announces solution for internet blackouts and network outages - Terminal records offline transaction, transmits when the connection is restored - No card swapping: simply reconfigure readers in stores
## Key facts - **What**: Offline payments with physical cards and PINs at stores - When: Gradual implementation; wide diffusion by the end of 2027 - Where: Switzerland (first Central European country with a shared solution) - Who: DEFR, Swiss National Bank (SNB), Federal Council, business representatives - Mode: Local recording of the transaction, synchronization when the network is restored - Requirements: Physical cards with PINS; terminals powered by current or external battery in blackout - Impact: No paper replacement necessary, just reconfigure the readers
The Federal Department of the Economy (DEFR) announced today in Bern a statement of intent aimed at ensuring payments in stores even during internet outages or network blackouts. The solution was presented by business representatives at an event attended by the president of the Confederation Guy Parmelin, the president of the Swiss National Bank (SNB) Martin Schlegel and the delegate to the Economic Supply of the Country Roland Pfister.
Implementation will take place gradually, with the aim of achieving wide dissemination by Switzerland thus joins the list of European countries that have decided to invest in the resilience of the national digital payment system. Sweden has already implemented offline payments for some time, while other Northern European states such as Finland, Norway and Estonia are introducing similar measures. However, the DEFR stresses that Switzerland is the first Central European country to adopt a widely shared solution to strengthen the resilience of electronic payments.
### The impact on consumers' daily lives
For those who live and work in Switzerland, the change will bring significant practical benefits. Until now, any internet outage — be it due to technical failures, bad weather or emergencies — could completely block the possibility of buying goods with paper, forcing customers to resort to cash. With offline payments, the store will continue to operate normally, recording the transaction locally and processing it later.
This also has important repercussions on food security and essential services. During a blackout, basic necessities can still be purchased with a credit or debit card, keeping the [costo della vita](nav:cost-of-living) stable without forcing dependence on cash. The consumer will no longer have to carry significant amounts of money in times of infrastructure crisis.

item.description: From 2027 you can pay by card even without internet in Swiss stores. The DEFR adopts a new offline system to ensure continuity during blackouts.

## In a nutshell - Offline card payments from 2027: they also work without internet - The terminal records the transaction and transmits it to the network restore - Switzerland is the first Central European country; Sweden already uses this technology - Cards should not be replaced, just reconfigure the readers
## Key facts - **What**: Measure for offline payments in stores with credit/debit cards - When: By the end of 2027, widespread - Where: Switzerland, announced in Bern - Who: DEFR, business representatives, Guy Parmelin (Federal Council), Martin Schlegel (SNB), Roland Pfister (Economic Supply Delegate) - Mode: Payment with PIN on physical card; terminal records and transmits when the network is restored - Power supply: Card reader must be powered (battery/generator in case of blackout)
### A Statement of Intent for Payment Resilience
The Federal Department of the Economy has announced a statement of intent that will ensure the continuity of electronic payments even during internet blackouts or outages. The goal is to allow customers in Swiss stores to pay by credit or debit card even without a connection, by the end of 2027.
The event held in Bern was attended by the President of the Confederation Guy Parmelin, the President of the Swiss National Bank Martin Schlegel, the Delegate for Economic Supply Roland Pfister and representatives of companies. ### Switzerland follows the Nordic model
The offline payment system is not an absolute novelty. Sweden has been using it for years, responding to concerns about the resilience of digital infrastructure during critical outages. Countries such as Finland, Norway and Estonia are introducing similar measures.
With this mission statement, Switzerland becomes the first Central European country to adopt a widely shared and coordinated solution to strengthen the resilience of electronic payments. According to the Federal Department of Economics, the Swiss approach is distinguished by the consensus reached between the public sector (Federal Council, SNB) and the private sector (business representatives).
### Concrete implications for merchants and customers
Owners of small and medium-sized Swiss stores will be able to continue to cash out even when the telecommunications network is interrupted — a guarantee of sales continuity in the event of an emergency. Customers will not have to fear being cut off from their payments during a blackout.
However, the diffusion of the solution requires a double effort. On the one hand, payment terminals must be reconfigured. On the other hand, card readers must have an alternative power source (battery or generator) to operate during power outages. For those who do not have backup batteries, the solution is not automatic and requires investment.

Store owners who wish to adopt the offline payment system must begin evaluating their current payment terminals. Reconfiguring the card readers is the first step. It is not necessary to purchase new devices (in most cases), but it is essential for specialized technicians to reconfigure the firmware and security systems to enable offline mode.
The second step concerns backup power. Every terminal must have access to an external battery or a generator during blackouts. Merchants will therefore need to plan for: - The purchase of UPS (uninterruptible power supply systems) or portable batteries for the terminals - Periodic maintenance of these devices - Staff training on how to handle offline payments manually if necessary
For customers, communication is crucial. Store owners should signal on social media, websites, and with in-store signs that offline payments will be available. Many customers are unaware of this option and might fear being unable to pay during a blackout. A clear communication campaign will reduce anxiety and increase trust in the system.
### Timeline and available resources
By the end of 2027, the EAER estimates that the solution will see 'widespread adoption' in Switzerland. However, not all stores will be ready at the same time. Small businesses may proceed more slowly than large chains, which have dedicated IT resources.
It is advisable for merchants to inquire with their payment terminal providers about the timing and costs of reconfiguration. Local trade associations will be able to provide sector-specific guidelines and technical support during the transition.

To stay updated on this evolution and the implications for your financial management, it is useful to follow the communications of the EAER and the SNB. item.description: Complete guide to cantonal and municipal taxes in the canton of Basel-Country: rates, allowable deductions, reporting deadlines and online tax portal.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Tax system at 3 levels: federal (IFD) + cantonal + municipal - Progressive rates on taxable income brackets - Annual declaration within cantonal deadlines; online portal available - Municipalities apply a multiplier on the cantonal basis
## Key facts - **What**: Taxation on income, wealth and capital in the canton - Where: Canton Basel-Country (North-West Switzerland) - Who: Residents and people with income from cantonal source - Levels: Federal (IFD) + cantonal + municipal - Deductions: Professional expenses, AVS/LPP contributions, LAMal premiums according to federal law
### 3-level tax structure in the canton of Basel-Country The tax system of the Canton of Basel-Country is structured on three levels of taxation: the direct federal tax (IFD) paid to the Confederation and managed by the Federal Tax Administration (AFC), the cantonal tax administered by the regional tax office, and the municipal tax collected by the individual municipalities of the canton according to a fixed multiplier on the cantonal tax base. Each level applies progressive rates on the various brackets of taxable income, determined after the application of deductions allowed by federal legislation and specific cantonal provisions. Taxpayers resident in the canton are obliged to submit an annual tax return within the deadlines set by the cantonal administration, indicating income from employment and ### Practical implications for residents of the Canton of Basel-Country Those who reside in the canton of Basel-Country and receive income from any source are subject to taxation at all three levels: federal, cantonal and municipal. The total annual tax burden therefore depends both on the cantonal rate set by regional legislation and on the multiplier applied by the municipality of residence. Taxpayers with the same income but residing in different municipalities of the canton of Basel-Country will pay different municipal taxes, sometimes to a significant extent. For this reason, it is useful to check the municipal multiplier of your municipality and calculate the total tax burden starting from the net tax base after all allowable deductions. A preliminary estimate before the declaration makes it possible to organise the payment and assess the effect of additional deductions (e.g. voluntary payments to the third pillar 3a) on the net tax due.
### Differences between declaration of employees and independent workers Employees have income taxed directly by the employer, who pays tax advances according to cantonal calendars (usually monthly or quarterly). The cantonal tax administration verifies the payment of advances and settles the differences at the end of the tax year. Self-employed persons and business owners must submit a complete declaration with accounting annexes and detailed administrative management,
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure step-by-step for the cantonal tax declaration For those residing in the Canton Basel-Landschaft and required to submit the annual declaration, the process follows these concrete steps:
**Phase 1: Collecting documentation** — Gather pay slips received, bank statements, AVS/LPP payment receipts, professional expense justifications (if self-employed), LAMal/KVG premium payment attestations during the year, documentation of donations to recognized institutions, bank account statements and investment records if subject to wealth taxation.
Phase 2: Authentication on the online portal — Reach the official website of the cantonal tax administration and authenticate with personal credentials (federal social insurance number + password, or digital signature via Swiss e-banking). The portal is available in German and French; informative texts, downloadable forms, and guides are available in Italian at the counters or upon request.
Phase 3: Filling out the declaration — Enter gross income, deduct documented expenses, indicate AVS/LPP payments made, LAMal premiums paid, and other allowed deductions. The system automatically calculates the cantonal and communal tax based on the net taxable income and applicable legislation.
Phase 4: Attaching justifications — Digitally upload required documents (pay slips, receipts, bank statements) within the file size limit set by the portal.
Phase 5: Submission and confirmation — Submit the digitally signed declaration. The portal generates a receipt with the date and time of submission; a copy remains archived in the personal account.
Phase 6: Monitoring the status — Periodically access the portal to verify the evaluation status and receive communication of the result (tax due, refund, or zero payment).
### Terms of delivery and administrative contacts The ordinary deadline for submitting the cantonal declaration is typically set between April and May of the following year of income; exact deadlines are communicated by the cantonal tax administration in documents sent to the taxpayer and visible on the official online portal. Extensions are granted upon motivated request submitted within the set terms. For clarifications on specific cantonal tax rates, allowed deductions in the canton, technical issues with accessing the portal, or other administrative matters, it is possible to contact the cantonal administration's counters in the detached capitals, the dedicated phone number for tax support (retrievable from the official website), or the email service of the tax office for non-urgent communications.
### Fiscal planning tools and tax estimates Many taxpayers use online calculators provided by federal entities (AFC) or the canton itself, where they can enter gross income and receive an accurate estimate of the total tax due (federal + cantonal + communal). This tool allows them to evaluate the concrete effect of additional deductions (third pillar 3a voluntary payments to a third-party pillar, professional pension contributions) on the net tax due and plan in advance for payment. Conscious fiscal planning enables taxpayers to avoid end-of-year surprises and identify legitimate opportunities for reducing their tax burden in compliance with federal and cantonal legislation.

The inheritance and gift tax in the Canton of Basel-City is a cantonal tax that affects the transfer of assets free of charge, both by inheritance and by donation. Unlike [imposta federale diretta, che è uniforme in tutta la Svizzera](nav:calculator), inheritance and gift taxes are governed entirely by cantonal laws: each Swiss canton has its own tax regimes, with rates and exemptions defined by its own legislation.
In the Canton of Basel-City, as in all cantons, the tax is divided according to the degree of kinship between the deceased (or donor) and the heir (or donor). The closer the relationship ### Rates, exemptions and degrees of kinship in the Canton Basel-City
In the Canton of Basel-City, as in the rest of Switzerland, taxation is divided into stages according to the degree of kinship. The main grades are organized as follows:
**First Degree (Spouse and Children)**: The surviving spouse generally benefits from substantial tax protection. In many Swiss cantons, including the Canton of Basel-City, the spouse enjoys a total exemption or a significantly reduced rate. Similarly, children and direct descendants benefit from very low rates or partial exemptions, reflecting their order of priority in Swiss civil law.
Second degree (parents, brothers, sisters): Relatives in the second degree of kinship are subject to moderate rates, higher than those reserved for the spouse and children, but lower than those of the most distant degrees.
Third grade (grandparents, uncles, cousins) and higher grades: These subjects benefit from an even higher rate. Persons without kinship (friends, acquaintances, strangers) are subject to the maximum rates provided for by cantonal law.
To consult the exact rates applicable in the Canton of Basel-City, it is essential to contact the cantonal tax administration directly, as these rates may be subject to legislative changes and vary not only by degree of kinship, but also by amount brackets.

If you have been appointed as an heir or have received an inheritance in the City of Basel, you must follow a formal procedure to fulfill your tax obligations. Here are the main steps to follow:
Phase 1: Gather Essential Documents
Obtain the following documents: - Original will (if exists) or certificate of intestate succession - Death certificate of the deceased (extract from the register) - Documents related to the inherited assets (bank statements, stock certificates, real estate deeds, insurance policies) - Documentation regarding debts or liabilities of the inheritance (mortgages, credits, funeral expenses) - Marriage or birth certificates to prove the degree of kinship
Phase 2: Contact the Cantonal Tax Administration
Contacting the City of Basel's tax office is a crucial step. Reach out to the administration to: - Request the official forms for the inheritance declaration - Clarify the submission deadlines (usually within a few months of the death, but verify exactly) - Obtain specific information on the applicable tax rates for your degree of kinship - Understand if you are entitled to exemptions or reliefs
Phase 3: Complete the Inheritance Declaration
Fill out the official form, providing: - Personal details of the deceased (name, date of death, last residence) - Complete list of heirs and legatees with indication of the degree of kinship - Detailed inventory of all assets (active and passive) - Market value of each asset at the time of death - Total value of the inheritance and taxable base
**Phase 4: Submission and Payment**
Submit the declaration within the specified deadline at the cantonal tax office (in person, by mail, or through the digital platform, as indicated by the administration). The office will notify the amount of tax due based on the applicable tax rate for your degree of kinship. Payment must be made within the terms indicated in the notification.
### Deadlines and Terms for Declaration
The deadlines for the inheritance declaration in the City of Basel vary depending on the current cantonal legislation and must be verified with the tax administration, as they may be subject to changes.
In general: - The declaration must be submitted within a few months of the death (the exact deadline varies - contact the office to confirm) - [The notification of the amount due follows after the submission of the declaration](nav:tax-return) - The tax payment must be made within the deadline indicated in the notification - Failure to comply with the deadlines may result in administrative penalties, interest, and potential coercive recovery procedures
Therefore, it is essential to act promptly and contact the tax administration as soon as possible after the death.

Given the complexity of the matter and the variability of inheritance situations, it may be advisable to consult specialized professionals: - Notary: for issues of will validity, interpretation of the testator's will, and succession law - Tax consultant or accountant: for accurate tax calculation, form completion, and tax planning - Lawyer specializing in succession law: for disputes between heirs or complex legal issues - Cantonal administration: for clarification on tax rates, exemptions, deadlines, and updated forms

## In a nutshell - Opening a business requires a choice of legal form (company, SA, SAGL, simple company) - Compulsory registration in the commercial register of the canton of Basel-City - Social contributions (AVS/AI 10.6%, AD 1.1%, LAMal) mandatory immediately - Federal, cantonal and municipal taxes in three levels
## Key facts - **What**: Registration in the trade register for new economic activities - Where: Canton of Basel-City (cantonal administration) - Who: Individual entrepreneurs, partners, shareholders according to legal form - When: Before starting economic activity - Legal forms: Sole proprietorship, simple company, SA, SAGL, cooperative - Taxes: Three-level system — federal (IFD), cantonal, municipal - Compulsory contributions: AVS/AI 10.6%, AD 1.1%, private LAMal, LPP if employees
Opening a business in the canton of Basel-City means facing an administrative and fiscal system structured on three levels of taxation and numerous social security obligations. The initial choice concerns the legal form: the tax regime, minimum capital requirements and insurance charges vary significantly between sole proprietorships, partnerships, public limited companies (SAs) and limited liability companies (SAGS).
The first concrete step is the registration in the commercial register of the canton of Basel-City. It is not an optional requirement: every economic activity exercised in a professional capacity must be registered before ### The Swiss tax system: three levels
Taxation in Switzerland consists of three distinct levels: direct federal tax (DFI), cantonal tax and municipal tax. Basel City, as a semi-canton, has its own cantonal multipliers and Basel municipalities apply municipal multipliers on a cantonal basis. This means that two businesses with the same turnover in different municipalities of Basel City can pay slightly different amounts of municipal tax, although the federal and cantonal basis remains identical.
A **SA** will pay corporate net income taxes at the three levels according to the federal progressive rates, the cantonal rate of Basel City and the specific municipal multiplier. A sole proprietorship will pay personal professional net income taxes, reducing the tax base with deductions for mandatory social contributions (AVS/AI, unemployment insurance) and documented professional expenses. A SAGL combines elements of both: the entity is taxed on income, but with greater distributional flexibility than an SA.
### Social security and insurance obligations
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for anyone residing in Switzerland and must be taken out within 3 months of the start of residence or the start of business for those who already reside. LAMal is not a tax or a salary contribution: it is a private insurance with per capita premiums that vary by canton and sick fund. Basel
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-Step Procedure for Registration
**Phase 1: Preliminary Preparation**
Before contacting the commercial register, define the legal form of your activity. If you choose a sole proprietorship, you will need a business name (denomination), the company address (Swiss address), and a brief description of the activity. If you choose a SA or SAGL, you must draw up a statute or founding deed, designate administrative bodies (board of directors, manager), and pay the minimum capital to a bank (depositary trustee). The simple partnership requires a written agreement between partners.
Phase 2: Registration with the Cantonal Office
The canton of Basel City has a central office for the commercial register where you can submit the registration application. At the national level, information on uniform procedures is coordinated between cantonal administrations, but the actual request is made to the cantonal office. Typical documents include: - Completed registration form (available at the cantonal office) - Bank certificate (if capital payment) - Statute/founding deed (for SA, SAGL, simple partnership) - Designation of administrators and legal representatives with authenticated signature - Identity document of the applicant
Phase 3: Notification to Tax and Insurance Authorities
After registration with the commercial register, the Federal Administration of Customs and Taxes (AFC) automatically receives the data from the cantonal database. However, you must notify your cantonal residence of the tax situation (federal and cantonal declarations) and conclude health insurance within 3 months. If you have employees, you must also register the company with the competent administrative office for professional pension management (LPP) for your sector and canton.
Phase 4: Opening a Bank Account and Accounting
Open a bank account in the company's name (SA/SAGL) or in your name (sole proprietorship). If your activity has invoiced above a certain limit, you may need to request a VAT number from the AFC for invoicing and paying the value-added tax. The accounting must be regularly updated and kept for at least 7 years for potential tax audits.
### Deadlines and Recurring Obligations
After registration, annual obligations include: - Federal and cantonal tax declarations: within the terms set by the AFC and canton (typically spring/summer of the following year) - Payment of AVS/AI, AD contributions: according to the calendar of the Commercial Register Office and cantonal administration - Payment of LPP contributions (if employees are registered): monthly to the company's pension fund - Balance sheet declaration (for SA, SAGL; less stringent for sole proprietorship): within 6 months of the end of the year - LAMal renewal and annual verification of cantonal subsidies
### Tools for Calculating Your Tax Burden
Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the impact of different levels of gross income and see how the withholding system (AVS, AD, federal and cantonal taxes) affects the net available. This simulation helps understand if the overall cost structure is sustainable.
To understand the context of living costs in the canton of Basel City and Switzerland in general, consult the guide on [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living). Remember that each canton has margins of maneuver on cantonal tax rates, and common ones apply their own multipliers.
For details on [pension and retirement](nav:pension), consult the guide dedicated to AVS/LPP calculations for self-employed workers. For [health insurance](nav:health), check the updated LAMal premiums in your canton and the conditions for subsidies.
Next step: Contact the Commercial Register Office of Basel City for the updated registration form, or consult a tax advisor familiar with local fiscal dynamics. Initial investment in a brief consultation will save you costly errors in administration and tax declarations.

item.title: Crowded skies in summer: 240,000 flights to Switzerland
item.description: From 26 June to 17 August Skyguide monitored 240,108 flights. On July 24, the record day with 4,761 movements.

## In a nutshell - 240,108 flights monitored between June and August 2026 - Peak on July 24: 4,761 flights in a single day - 93% of flights complied with planned schedules
## Key facts - **What**: Air traffic monitoring during summer holidays - When: 26 June - 17 August 2026 - Where: Swiss airspace, Zurich and Geneva airports - Who: Skyguide (Swiss air traffic control authority) - Amount of movements: 240,108 total flights; 44,485 in Zurich, 25,514 in Geneva - Punctuality: 93% of flights on time - Delays: 63% due to weather phenomena
During the 2026 summer holidays, Swiss airspace experienced unprecedented congestion. Between June 26 and August 17, Skyguide, the federal air traffic control authority, monitored a total of 240,108 flights. A figure that reflects the strong mobility of the Swiss during the summer period.
Traffic was not uniform. The peaks were concentrated on Fridays and Mondays, when people leave for the holidays or return home. The most congested day was July 24, with 4,761 flights monitored in the national airspace. If these planes were arranged in a row, maintaining the standard distance of five nautical miles between one plane and another, the tail would reach a length greater than a full circle of the Earth.
On average, during the summer, air traffic control handled 4,503 flights per day. Two hubs have been particularly pressed: Zurich Airport What makes July 24 a day to remember in Swiss skies? The combination of factors: it is a Friday, the weekly peak, and it falls in the heart of the summer holidays when schools and companies have already closed and families move to destinations.
The distribution of almost 4,761 movements in a single day has concrete implications for those who move. Peak times — early morning and late afternoon — concentrate the bulk of take-offs. Those who fly during these times face greater risks of waiting at the gate, delays in taxiing and congestion in the cruise airspace.
### Strategies to avoid critical days
Skyguide data suggests a definite trend: Mondays and Fridays are critical-critical. If your trip allows flexibility, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays offer significantly less traffic. July, in general, is also more congested than June: anticipating the start can reduce the pressure. Those who evaluate alternatives, perhaps using the [trasporti pubblici](nav:transport) for destinations reachable by train, find additional travel options without air congestion.
Punctuality remains strong (93%), but 7% of delays are still relevant: on a day like July 24 with 4,761 flights, about 333 movements suffered disruptions. If you are a passenger connecting flights or have important deadlines, these numbers are worth considering.

If your trip falls in August or you are forced to fly on a Friday, here is what you can do to minimize disruptions.
Step 1: Consult the Skyguide calendar. Although Skyguide historical data does not predict future days with exact precision, the pattern is well established — Fridays and Mondays remain critical. Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays are quieter days.
Step 2: Choose off-peak times. If you fly on July 24, avoid 7-9 AM and 4-6 PM. Evening flights (after 8 PM) generally experience less congestion and often slightly lower fares, positively impacting the overall [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) of your vacation.
Step 3: Monitor weather forecasts. Since 63% of summer delays are caused by weather phenomena, checking the weather a week before your flight is essential. Thunderstorms and fog are the main disruption factors.
Step 4: Add connection time. If you are booking connecting flights, especially on peak days, allow at least 2-3 hours between landing and the next takeoff. The 7% of summer delays can compromise tight connection times.
### Useful information
Skyguide regularly publishes data on Swiss airspace congestion. Frequent flyers or those managing complex schedules (business travel, logistics) can consult official reports to optimize routes and schedules.
For vacation planners, the lesson is simple: if you are flexible, shift your flight by a day or a few hours and drastically reduce the risk of waiting. If you have no choice, plan for extra buffers and check the weather.
In Switzerland, thanks to the quality air traffic control system, flights generally remain reliable: a 93% on-time rate is an encouraging figure. Starting an activity in the Basel-City Canton means dealing with a regulatory system divided into three levels: federal, cantonal and municipal. Those who decide to launch themselves into entrepreneurship must face crucial choices about the company structure before even counting the final costs.

The consequence is that two identical companies in different cantons pay different taxes. There is no single national tax: the IFD (direct federal tax) is managed by the Confederation (AFC - Federal Tax Administration/ ESTV) as a federal level, while cantonal and municipal taxes remain the responsibility of the local cantonal administration.
For a personal company or an SA, the tax is calculated annually on the basis of the declared gross income/profit. item.title: Buying a house in Basel City: mortgage and costs
item.description: Practical guide to buying real estate in the canton of Basel-City: mortgage financing, transfer taxes, notary fees and step-by-step procedure. Where to inquire for specific local data.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Buying a house in Switzerland requires own funds and a mortgage regulated by the SNB - Transfer tax and notary fees are the responsibility of the canton, vary by canton and municipality - Uniform federal procedure: preliminary, financing, notarial deed, land registration
## Key facts - **What**: Purchase of residential property in Switzerland through mortgage - Who: Buyers, banks (finance mortgages), notaries (deed), Land Registry Office - Where: Canton Basel City - When: Total procedure from 4-8 weeks prior to registration - Own funds: Typically 10-20% of the purchase price (not uniform at the federal level) - Regulation: Federal mortgages (SNB); cantonal transfer taxation and land taxes
Buying a house in Basel City follows the established rules of the Swiss real estate market: a combination of private finance (own funds and mortgage loan), cantonal taxation (transfer tax) and standardized federal procedures (notarial deed, registration in the land register). Unlike in Italy, where the purchase of real estate is subject to uniform national taxes, in Switzerland the taxation on the transfer of ownership is exclusive to the cantons and municipalities. This means that the costs of a purchase in Basel City differ significantly from Zurich, Geneva or Lausanne.
Real estate financing is done through a mortgage loan: Swiss banks, subject to regulations ### Transfer tax in Switzerland: cantonal competence
The transfer tax on immovable property — also known as "transfer tax" or "registration fee" — is a tax levied on the sale of real estate. Unlike the federal direct tax (national rate) or VAT (federal competence), the transfer tax is exclusive to cantons and municipalities: each canton decides whether to introduce the tax, at what rate, and with what exemptions. The Canton of Basel City, like all Swiss cantons, has its own tax law that regulates the transfer tax. The rate varies depending on the ratio of sale price to cadastral value, as well as the type of buyer (natural person, company, entity). Some cantons exempt transfers between close relatives — parents-children, spouses — while others apply full rates.
The tax is calculated on the sale price agreed upon by the parties and recorded in the notarized deed. There is no uniform percentage: some cantons apply progressive rates (increasing with price), others fixed. The notary who draws up the deed is required to calculate the tax and notify the cantonal tax offices. A property purchased in Basel City does not incur the same rates as one purchased in Zurich or Ticino. This is why the search for the right home must take into account not only the geographical location and price, but also the local tax burden. To understand the impact of property taxes on your personal situation, consult the [tax return](nav:tax-return) and check with the Basel City cantonal tax office for specific details applicable.
### Notary fees, registration, and other costs
In addition to the transfer tax, the buyer bears non-recurring costs to complete the purchase. Notary fees — the notary's fee for drawing up the deed — are not fixed at the federal level but vary by canton and notary, as the notary market is liberalized. Typically, notary fees range from 0.5% to 1.5% of the purchase price, an estimate that requires direct consultation with local notaries in Basel City for precision.
Registration in the land register is mandatory by federal law (Swiss Civil Code, art. 960 seq.). Once the deed is drawn up, the property must be registered in the cantonal land register (Grundbuch in German). Registration fees vary: some cantons require a few dozen CHF, while others apply percentages of 0.1-0.3% of the price. Home insurance (contents and structure) is mandatory in almost every canton. The premium depends on the value of the property, geographical location, and insurance risk profile. Once the owner, the buyer pays an annual property tax (land tax), calculated on the cadastral or market value of the property. This is cantonal/municipal competence and varies significantly: some municipalities have high rates (1-2% of the value), while others are low.
### Tax deductibility: what is deductible
Are non-recurring acquisition costs deductible from taxes? It depends on Basel City legislation. Normally, notary fees and registration fees are not deductible from federal direct taxes (IFD); however, some cantons allow partial deductions from cantonal/municipal taxes. It is essential to verify with the Basel City cantonal tax office. Annual land taxes, on the other hand, are always deductible from federal direct taxes up to certain limits (standard deduction for owner-occupiers).
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-Step Procedure: How to Buy a House in Switzerland
The procedure for buying a property in Switzerland follows a standardized federal path, with cantonal variations:
**1. Search and Preliminary Offer** Identify the desired house, the buyer makes a verbal or written offer. The price is completely negotiable. If the seller accepts the offer, the parties sign a non-binding preliminary agreement or a memorandum of sale outlining the main terms.
2. Financing: Bank Approval The buyer contacts one or more Swiss banks (the market is competitive: request quotes from 3-4 institutions) for a mortgage offer. The bank requires: ID and proof of residence, last 2-3 pay stubs, tax return, bank statement to verify available assets, independent property inspection, and registry certificate. After 2-3 weeks of evaluation, the bank issues a mortgage offer with an indicative interest rate, term, maximum amount, and explicit sustainability conditions.
3. Resolution and Notarial Deed Upon bank approval, the buyer and seller agree on a notarization date (usually 4-8 weeks after offer acceptance). The notary drafts the sale deed with public signature, describing the cadastral data, agreed price, payment methods, and mortgage charge (the mortgage pledge). The parties sign in the presence of the notary.
4. Payment and Property Transfer The bank transfers the mortgage to the seller's lawyer or notary's account. The buyer pays their own funds. The notary verifies the total balance and authorizes the property transfer.

item.title: Permit C Basel City: rights and naturalization requirements
item.description: Residence permit C in the Canton of Basel City: 10 years residence (5 EU/EFTA), federal integration, cantonal procedure and path to Swiss ordinary naturalization.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The C permit is the federal permanent residence permit for foreigners in Switzerland - Minimum requirement: 10 years continuous residence (5 for EU/EFTA citizens) - Basel City manages local integration procedure and criteria according to federal law - Permit C paves the way towards ordinary Swiss naturalisation
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit C (federal permanent residence permit) - When: Release normally after ≥10 years residence (5 for EU/EFTA) - Where: Canton Basel City (cantonal competence for procedure and integration) - Who: Federal SEM Administration + cantonal authorities Basel City - Requirements: Continuous residence, absence of public safety hazards, basic integration
Residence permit C is the most important federal title for foreigners who wish to settle permanently in Switzerland. At the national level, federal law normally provides for issuance after 10 years of continuous residence, or after 5 years for citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). In the Canton of Basel-City, as in all Swiss cantons, this federal competence is administered in synergy with cantonal requirements, which include integration criteria and compliance with local regulations.
Permit C represents the fundamental step towards lasting legal stability: it allows unlimited residence, facilitates access to the labour market without ### Cantonal procedure in Basel-City: how it works
In the Canton of Basel-City, the C permit is administered by the competent cantonal migration office (part of the cantonal police structure or department of justice). The application is not automatic: after meeting the minimum residency requirement, the resident foreign national must submit a formal application to the local authorities.
The cantonal procedure, although following federal principles, includes specific verification steps: the cantonal administration checks municipal registries to certify 10 years (or 5 for EU/EFTA) of uninterrupted residency. Subsequently, the SEM and cantonal authorities verify whether the applicant has a clean criminal record and does not pose a security threat. Basel-City, like other cantons, evaluates integration through specific criteria: knowledge of German (the official language of the canton), participation in the labor market, and absence of dependence on social welfare. Following complete verification, the canton issues the C permit, normally valid for 10 years and renewable.
Generally, the procedure takes between 3 and 6 months, depending on the cantonal administrative workload. Federal law provides for cases of early issuance: the C permit may be granted before 10 years (or 5 for EU/EFTA) in special situations such as marriage to a Swiss citizen (required residency reduced to 3-5 years in cantons that allow it), children of Swiss citizens (more favorable criteria), or employees of companies of federal significance (rarely). Basel-City may apply these exceptions, but the details remain in the hands of the local cantonal administration.
### What changes in life after the C permit
With the C permit, you gain access to rights that the B permit (temporary residence) does not grant: complete freedom of movement (you can change canton or city of residence without prior authorization, although you must register with local authorities). Access to the labor market becomes unlimited: no professional restrictions; you can look for work in any sector. Social rights expand: access to cantonal social subsidies and benefits, although with some limitations based on citizenship and duration of residency. For the [tax return](nav:tax-return) and other fiscal aspects, your permanent residence is legally recognized at the federal level, simplifying procedures and transparency. Finally, social security contributions become mandatory: you contribute to AVS/AHV (old-age and survivors insurance) and AI (disability insurance) with a rate of 5.3% for employees (10.6% total including the employer). If employed, LPP/BVG (occupational pension insurance) with a variable rate (7% between 25-34 years, 10% between 35-44 years, 15% between 45-54 years, 18% from 55 years until the reference age) also becomes binding.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure to apply for a C permit in Basel-City
**Step 1: Check the prerequisites**. Ensure you have reached 10 years of uninterrupted residency in Switzerland (or 5 if you are an EU/EFTA citizen). Check your municipal registry for the exact registration date and keep official documentation.
Step 2: Gather documentation. You will need to submit a valid passport or identity card, criminal record extracts (from your country of origin and Switzerland, if applicable), a recently issued municipal residence certificate, an employment document (employment contract) or tax return, and proof of language proficiency (diplomas, certificates, or a simple declaration, depending on the canton of Basel-City practice).
Step 3: Contact the competent office. The exact address depends on the cantonal administration of Basel-City. Generally, it is the Cantonal Police (Department of Justice and Security) or a specific immigration office. Check the official portal of the canton.
Step 4: Submit the application. It can be submitted in person at the office, by mail, or via the cantonal online portal (if available).
Step 5: Wait for verification. The canton will carry out residency, security, and integration checks. Remain available for any interviews or requests for additional documents. It is normal to receive requests for clarification during this period.
Step 6: Receive the issuance. Once approved, you will receive the C permit in the form of a federal legitimization card or digital document according to cantonal procedures.
### The path to ordinary Swiss naturalization
Residency permit C paves the way for ordinary Swiss naturalization, which represents the next step for those wishing to acquire Swiss citizenship. At the federal level, the minimum requirements are: possession of permit C, at least 10 years of residency in Switzerland (with favorable counting: years between 18 and 22 count double, reducing the effective time). However, naturalization is not a completely automatic federal procedure: each canton and sometimes each municipality has its own procedures and criteria. In Basel-City, as elsewhere, the procedure generally takes 6-18 months and may include in-depth historical, civic, or language knowledge tests.
To learn more about how permit C impacts your tax and social security position in Switzerland, consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator), which helps you understand the impact of federal, cantonal, and municipal taxation on your gross income. To check how OASI (AVS) and occupational pension (LPP) work after the issuance of permit C, access the [social security guide](nav:pension).

item.title: Residence permit B Basel City: requirements and renewal
item.description: Practical guide to the renewable residence permit in the Canton of Basel-City: requirements, documents, duration, renewal procedure and contacts of the migration office.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit B = renewable stay for foreigners in Switzerland - Each canton has autonomy over requirements and procedures - Basel City manages the release through cantonal migration office - Different from permit L (short duration) and C (domicile)
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit category B (renewable) - Where: Canton of Basel-City, north-western Switzerland - Who: Basel City Cantonal Migration Office - Type: SEM category B - Duration: Renewable (specific for canton)
In the Canton of Basel-City, the category B residence permit represents the renewable residence permit for foreigners wishing to settle in Switzerland. Managed by the cantonal migration office, this permit is part of the SEM system that regulates the entry and stay of foreign nationals throughout Switzerland. Unlike other residence permits, the B permit is characterised by its renewability, allowing those who hold it to extend their residence permit at the end of its validity.
### Permit B in the Swiss SEM system
In Switzerland, the stay of foreigners is regulated by the SEM permit system, which provides for four main categories. The L permit is intended for those who intend to stay for a short period, up to one year. The B permit, on the other hand, is designed for those who want a more stable and continuous residence, with characteristic renewability. Then there is permit C, intended Permit B vs permit C: practical differences
Those who plan to move to Switzerland often ask which type of permit is more suitable for their situation. The main differences between the permit of residence (category B) and the permit of domicile (category C) are significant both on the administrative and practical planes.
The permit B is renewable for limited periods and must be requested for renewal. The permit C, on the other hand, is intended for those who have accumulated a minimum period of residence in Switzerland: generally not less than 10 years for citizens of non-EU/EEA countries, and not less than 5 years for citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association. The permit C confers a more stable position and does not require periodic renewals in the same way.
Even from the point of view of geographical mobility, the two categories differ. The holder of a permit B must generally notify changes of domicile within the canton, and must renew the permit if they decide to move to another canton. The holder of a permit C has greater freedom of movement within Switzerland.
From the point of view of access to social services and healthcare, both permit B and C holders have the right to coverage of [LAMal (mandatory health insurance)](nav:health), which is a private insurance with premiums per capita. In the Canton of Basel City, as in all cantons, LAMal is mandatory for all residents within 3 months of arrival. Cantonally subsidized premiums for reducing premiums vary by canton and individual situation.
### Fiscal and pension implications
From a tax perspective, both permit B and C holders are subject to the Swiss three-tier tax system: federal direct tax (managed by AFC/ESTV), cantonal tax, and municipal tax. Each canton has its own rates and regulations, and municipalities apply a multiplier to cantonal tax. In the Canton of Basel City, specific rates must be checked with the competent cantonal tax administration.
Regarding social security, permit B holders who work in Switzerland are enrolled in the AVS/AI (old-age and disability insurance) system. Contributions are 5.3% for the employee and 10.6% in total with the employer. In addition, employees are subject to contributions for unemployment insurance (AD/AC), amounting to 1.1% up to an annual maximum.
Regarding the company pension fund (LPP/BVG), permit B holders who earn a coordinated salary have compulsory contributions that vary by age range: 7% for the 25-34 age range, 10% for 35-44 years, 15% for 45-54 years, and 18% for 55 years up to the reference age. These contributions are deducted directly from the salary.
### Family allocations and social rights
An important aspect concerns access to family allocations. Permit B holders who work in Switzerland and have children can access family allocations, the amount of which varies by canton. In addition, the permit B holder has the right to 2 weeks of paid leave for paternity insurance (federal right).
As for the insurance against work-related accidents (LAINF/LAA), this is mandatory for employees with permit B and amounts to around 0.7-1.5% of the salary depending on the sector. Insurance against occupational diseases is part of the same coverage.

Those wishing to relocate to the Canton of Basel City must follow a clear administrative procedure. The first step is to complete the application form provided by the cantonal migration office of Basel City. This form must be accompanied by the required documentation (identity document, residence certificate, police certificate, and any income documentation).
Once the application is submitted, the cantonal migration office examines the request and verifies compliance with the requirements. The processing time typically ranges from a few days to several weeks, depending on the complexity of the application and the office's workload. It is recommended to maintain regular contact with the office to check the status of the application.
After approval of the application, the B permit is issued with a validity and expiration date. The permit holder receives an official copy, which must be carefully preserved, as it is the document that attests the right to stay in Switzerland.
### Permit Renewal: Timelines and Documents
The renewal of the residence permit (category B) must be requested before the expiration date. Normally, the Canton of Basel City sends a reminder to the permit holder a few months before the expiration date, reminding them to renew. However, it is the permit holder's responsibility to check the expiration date on the permit.
To renew, you must:
- Submit a renewal request within the times set by the canton - Provide updated documentation (residence certificate, police certificate, and any income documentation) - Pay any applicable administrative renewal fee - Verify that the original conditions persist (residence in the canton, compliance with the law)
If the conditions persist and there are no issues with the application, the permit is renewed, and a new copy is issued valid for the next period.
### Contacts and Information at the Cantonal Migration Office
The cantonal migration office of Basel City is the primary point of contact for any questions related to the B permit. It is recommended to contact the office to verify specific requirements, obtain the updated list of required documents, know the submission deadlines, receive assistance in completing the application, and clarify any doubts about the renewal procedure.
Cantonal migration offices operate according to fixed opening hours and usually offer the possibility of phone, email, or in-person contact. It is recommended to check the contact details and hours before visiting the office.
### Support Tools: Fiscal and Social Security Information
Once the B permit is obtained, the permit holder must fulfill obligations such as registration with the local municipality and enrollment in the tax system. At the federal level, the Federal Administration of Customs and the Federal Tax Administration (ESTV) manage the federal direct tax and VAT. At the cantonal level (at the Basel City Tax Administration), practical compliance with cantonal and municipal taxes is managed.
Regarding social security, it is essential to verify enrollment in the AVS system at the Social Insurance Office (UFAS/BSV) and enrollment in the occupational pension fund (LPP) at the employer or relevant pension fund.

## In a nutshell - Permit B is a federal renewable home category managed by the SEM - Basel-City has a cantonal migration office for local processes - Renewal requires verification by SEM and cantonal authorities - Crucial distinction between permit L (short), B (medium), C (domicile)
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit B, federal renewable category (SEM) - Where: Canton of Basel-City (Basel-Stadt), Switzerland - Who: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) + cantonal authority Basel City - When: Renewal to be requested before the expiration of the document - Duration: Renewable according to federal criteria; specific duration refers to the SEM - Amount: Costs not yet specified in this guide
Permit B represents a federal category of residence in Switzerland, managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). Unlike the L permit (short duration, up to 1 year) and the C permit (domicile), the B permit offers an intermediate position: it allows you to stay and work in Switzerland with the possibility of renewing your residence permit. In the Canton of Basel-City, as in all Swiss cantons, the B permit renewal procedure follows federal guidelines, but also requires interaction with the local cantonal migration office.
Whoever obtains the B permit, moreover, is subject to Swiss tax obligations — for this reason it is useful to familiarize yourself with the [dichiarazione delle imposte](nav:tax-return) already at the moment ### Scenario di rinnovo: come funziona
Immaginiamo uno scenario tipico. A non-EU worker has obtained a B permit with an expiration date in autumn 2026. A few weeks before the expiration date, they must contact the cantonal migration office in Basel City to signal their intention to renew. The federal procedure provides that all renewal requests are examined by the SEM in coordination with the cantonal authorities. It is not possible to automatically extend the B permit: each renewal requires a formal request and verification that the requirements are still met.
### Comparison table: L vs B vs C
| Permit | Duration | Renewable | Access to the labor market | Way to home address | |----------|--------|-------------|-------------------------------|---------------------| | **L** | Up to 1 year | Limited | Yes, with restrictions | No | | B | Variable (federal) | Yes | Yes, extensive | Yes, after 10 years of residence | | C | 10 years (renewable) | Yes | Yes, complete | Already stable residence |
### Differences between L and B permits in renewal
The L permit, with a maximum duration of 1 year, is not intended for repeated renewals of the same holder in the medium term. It is a solution for episodic stays (seasonal work, short training, temporary project). On the other hand, the B permit is specifically designed for those who intend to settle in Switzerland for one or more years, with the awareness that renewal is a right as long as the federal and cantonal conditions (employment, economic resources, absence of security problems) continue to exist. The C permit, finally, is the culmination of the scale: it requires a 10-year stay (5 for EU/EFTA) and represents a stable residence with almost the same rights as Swiss citizens.
### What remains not yet specified
This guide provides the federal and cantonal framework. However, details such as the exact list of required documents, the costs of renewal, the specific duration of the B permit (which can vary depending on the employment contract and circumstances), and the exact address of the cantonal migration office in Basel City remain to be verified directly with the authorities. It is recommended to contact the SEM and the cantonal office of Basel to obtain personalized information.
Before requesting the B permit, also understand the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) in your destination canton: federal and cantonal authorities assess whether you have sufficient economic resources to maintain yourself legally during the stay.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-step towards renewal
The renewal process of the B permit follows some fundamental steps:
1. Check the expiration date of your B permit (visible on the document itself) 2. Contact the cantonal migration office of Basel City several months before the expiration date to notify the intention to renew 3. Prepare the required documentation (valid passport, proof of employment, proof of financial resources, proof of accommodation, certificate of non-existence of penal problems — check the exact list with the office) 4. Send or submit the renewal application to the cantonal office 5. Wait for the elaboration by the cantonal office and the SEM
### Contacts and next steps
The SEM is reachable through the official website of the Swiss Confederation for questions on federal procedures. In the Canton of Basel City, the migration office is the local point of contact for specific questions on renewal, required documents, and costs. We recommend contacting them by phone or email to obtain detailed and up-to-date information. Office hours and contact details are available on the official website of the Canton of Basel City.
### Practical implications
The renewal of the B permit is essential to maintain the legality of your residence and employment in Switzerland. A missed renewal application within the terms can lead to administrative complications, loss of the right to work, and obstacles for future permit applications. For those aspiring to the C permit (after 10 years of residence), maintaining compliance with B permit renewals is a crucial step towards stable residence.
### Calculate your numbers
If you are planning a stay in Switzerland, understanding the fiscal and income structure is just as important as the permit itself. ## In a nutshell - The Swiss labour market is divided into salary bands related to the degree of training (apprenticeship, diploma, university) - Collective agreements govern minimum wages, hours and contributions in many sectors - AVS/AI contributions (5.3%), LPP and LAMal are mandatory for each employee - Maximum hours: 45 hours per week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 hours (other sectors)
## Key facts - **What**: Cantonal employment structure with salary levels for training - Where: Canton of Solothurn, Switzerland - Who: Employees, employers, professional categories - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices) or 50 hours (other sectors) - Minimum holiday: 4 weeks per year (5 if under 20) - Maternity: 14 weeks at 80% of salary through allowance (IPG) - Paternity: 2 weeks paid
In the Canton of Solothurn, as in every Swiss canton, the labour market reflects a professional structure based on training levels and pay levels defined by federal law and cantonal ordinances. The search for employment and the determination of salaries follow precise rules that directly affect the paycheck, social security contributions and compulsory insurance.
### Salary bands by degree of training
The Swiss employment market is historically divided into three levels of qualification. The first is vocational apprenticeship (AFC — Federal Certificate ### Mandatory Contributions and Insurance Obligations
A worker's salary in the Canton of Solothurn consists of a gross part (the contractual salary) and a series of mandatory deductions. These reflect federal, cantonal contributions and insurance obligations established by Swiss laws.
**First Pillar: AVS/AI/IPG
The Old Age and Survivors Insurance (AVS), Disability Insurance (AI), and Maternity/Paternity Loss of Earnings Indemnity (IPG) constitute the first pillar of Swiss pension provision. The dependent worker pays 5.3% of the gross salary; the employer pays 10.6% in total (with its own share of 5.3%). These contributions finance public pensions: from 64 years for women (65 for men), the worker receives a monthly AVS pension based on contributions paid and years of work.
Unemployment
Unemployment contributions (AD — Unemployment Insurance; AC — Unemployment Insurance for the Worker's Fault) total 1.1% up to a yearly maximum, divided between the dependent and the employer. These payments ensure a daily allowance if the worker loses their job involuntarily.
Accidents at Work Insurance
The Work Accidents Insurance (LAINF) is paid by the employer to an insurance company (SUVA or recognized private insurers) and varies from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the activity sector. The employee does not contribute directly; the employer includes the cost in the operational budget.
### Second Pillar: Occupational Pension (LPP/BVG)
The Pension Fund (LPP — Law on Occupational Pension for Old Age, Survivors, and Disability) is mandatory for employees with an annual salary above a coordinated threshold (not included in this analysis, as it is annually indexed). The LPP operates on a defined contribution basis: the employer pays a percentage of the coordinated salary (gross salary minus a deduction), the employee another percentage. The rates increase with age:
- Age 25–34 years: 7% - Age 35–44 years: 10% - Age 45–54 years: 15% - Age 55+ up to the reference age (65 men, 64 women): 18%
These percentages apply to the coordinated salary, not the entire salary. The LPP accumulates individual capital during working life, paid out as a monthly pension at retirement or as a lump sum (according to the fund's choices).
### LAMal: Mandatory Health Insurance
Every resident in Switzerland must subscribe to a mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) within 3 months of arrival or starting work. Unlike AVS, LPP, and unemployment contributions, LAMal IS NOT a salary contribution. It is a private policy subscribed individually to a health fund (Helsana, CSS, Sanitas, Allianz, etc.) with a monthly or quarterly premium. The premium varies by canton, age range, sex, and annual franchise choice (CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, or 2,500). Many Swiss cantons, including Solothurn, reduce premiums for low-income residents through a cantonal subsidy.
### Practical Scenario: Impact on the Pay Slip
A dependent worker in the Canton of Solothurn with a gross salary of CHF 60,000 per year and an age between 35 and 44 years bears the following burdens:
- AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% = CHF 3,180 per year - Unemployment (AD/AC): approximately CHF 200–300 per year (maximum) - LPP (on a coordinated salary of approximately CHF 38,000): 10% = approximately CHF 3,800 per year - Federal direct tax: variable, depends on income, marital status, personal deductions - Solothurn cantonal tax: variable by municipality (own rates according to cantonal ordinance) - LAMal (estimated premium): CHF 300–600 per month, not deducted from the pay slip (paid directly to the health fund)

Local companies also publish offers on dedicated cantonal platforms, on the website of the Soletta-Nidvaldo Chamber of Commerce, and through Swiss placement agencies specialised by sector. item.title: Wages and market: sectors, training and contracts
